\chapter{Review --- The Pairs}
\label{ch:review-double-object}
\hlchaptermodality{101}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can generate every permitted pair of object pronouns from two facts.}

Complete ES-C47-repaso-dobles: state the two facts that generate the table and say how many new pronouns the arc added.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Review — the pairs}

\label{lesson:ES-C47-repaso-dobles}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new. Two facts before the table: which pronoun leads, and what happens to \emph{le} in front of \emph{lo}?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Every pair Spanish permits, in one place:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{+ thing} & \textbf{gives} \\
\midrule
me & lo / la / los / las & \textbf{me lo}, \textbf{me la}, \textbf{me los}, \textbf{me las} \\
te & " & \textbf{te lo}, \textbf{te la}, … \\
\textbf{le / les} & " & \textbf{se lo}, \textbf{se la}, \textbf{se los}, \textbf{se las} \\
nos & " & \textbf{nos lo}, \textbf{nos la}, … \\
os & " & \textbf{os lo}, \textbf{os la}, … \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the whole table as \textbf{two facts}, because that is all it is:

1. The person comes first. Always. 2. \emph{Le} and \emph{les} turn into \emph{se} in front of the thing. Only there.

Every other row is just the two pronouns you already had, standing next to each other with nothing done to either of them.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: how little is actually new}]
Count the new material in this whole arc: \textbf{one order, and one substitution.} No new pronoun, no new form, no new position in the sentence. Four chapters, two facts, and one of the two turned out to be an accident of medieval pronunciation rather than a rule at all.

That is worth saying plainly, because \emph{se lo} has a reputation. It is usually taught as the moment Spanish object pronouns become genuinely hard. It is instead the moment they stop growing: this is the last new thing the system does.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}me lo, te lo, se lo, nos lo, os lo\textquotedblright{} — the whole first column
  \item \textquotedblleft{}se lo digo, se la hago\textquotedblright{} and notice that only the middle row changed
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which row is the only one that changes? (\emph{\textbf{Le}} and \emph{\textbf{les}} $\to$ \emph{\textbf{se}}.) How many new pronouns did you learn here? (\textbf{None}.) Next: all of it in a conversation, at speed.
\end{tcolorbox}
